quote: Dennoch ist es nicht möglich zu entscheiden, ob $ax^3+b$ eine Primzahl darstellt, obwohl nur $F(a,b)$ Operationen dazu nothwendig wären. Dagegen wären wir völlig befriedigt, wenn etwa [-...-] $F(a,b) < a!\,b!$ nachweisbar wäre.
english: Nevertheless it is not possible to decide whether $ax^3+b$ represents a prime, although only $F(a,b)$ operations would be needed for it. On the other hand we would be completely satisfied if, say, $F(a,b) < a!\,b!$ could be proved.
topic: Philosophical and methodological remarks: linguistic intuition, the relativity of existence, the aim of science as ordering sensations, a critique of Kronecker's finitist demand illustrated by a prime-number example and Hilbert's finiteness proof for invariants, problem-posing in number theory, and the central place of number theory in mathematics.

triage.modern_statement: Take integers a, b and the cubic f(x) = ax^3 + b. Does f take at least one prime value at an integer x, and can this be decided by an algorithm whose search length is bounded in advance? In particular, is there an explicit bound F(a,b), for example a!·b!, such that if f takes a prime value at all, it already does so for some |x| ≤ F(a,b)? Hilbert uses the example to argue against Kronecker's finitist demand. If f does take a prime value, a blind search will eventually find it. But without a proven bound, the search can never establish that no prime value exists. In modern terms this is an effective version of the Bunyakovsky conjecture for cubic polynomials in one variable, i.e. an explicit upper bound for the smallest prime value of an irreducible cubic. If Bunyakovsky's conjecture were known, the question would be decidable: when f is reducible or has a fixed prime divisor, only finitely many values need checking, and otherwise f would take infinitely many prime values.
triage.answered_by: Nobody, as far as the sources I found show. Bunyakovsky's conjecture is still unproved for every polynomial of degree ≥ 2 in one variable. So there is no proof that any non-trivial cubic of the form ax^3 + b takes infinitely many prime values, and I found no unconditional general bound F(a,b) on its smallest prime value. The closest unconditional result is in two variables: D. R. Heath-Brown, 'Primes represented by x^3+2y^3', Acta Mathematica 186 (2001), 1–84. My searches did not turn up a published proof of a bound like F(a,b) < a!·b!, but they were not exhaustive. This note does not match any of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Bunyakovsky's conjecture says that an irreducible integer polynomial with positive leading coefficient and no fixed prime divisor takes infinitely many prime values. The only proven case is degree 1 (Dirichlet's theorem).
Not a single case of Bunyakovsky's conjecture of degree greater than one has been proved, although numerical evidence agrees with it.
Current work still treats the one-variable Bunyakovsky conjecture and its quantitative form, the Bateman–Horn conjecture, as open hypotheses.
Heath-Brown proved in 2001 that the two-variable cubic form x^3 + 2y^3 represents infinitely many primes. This is a related two-variable result, not the one-variable case Hilbert asks about.

The context: Hilbert's general finiteness proof for invariants (1890) was criticised as non-constructive, Gordan's 'theology' remark being the best-known reaction, and Hilbert answered with a second, more constructive paper in 1893. This is the kind of existence proof Hilbert is defending against Kronecker.

triage.why: Hilbert is not posing a new problem here. He is pointing to a gap in what is known and using it as a methodological example. Read precisely, his question is an effective form of the Bunyakovsky conjecture for one-variable cubics: an explicit bound on the smallest prime value of ax^3 + b, which would make 'does it represent a prime?' decidable. The sources show that no degree ≥ 2 case of Bunyakovsky has been proved, so the unconditional decidability Hilbert hoped for is still unavailable. Prime values of polynomials remain an active research area, with Bateman–Horn, sieve methods and Heath-Brown's two-variable results. Confidence is medium for three reasons. First, matching the note to Bunyakovsky is my reading of a short, partly illegible passage (the [-...-]). Second, it is unclear whether Hilbert meant a fixed x or the existence of some x. If he meant a fixed x, the question is just primality testing, which is decidable (and polynomial-time since AKS, 2002), and the note would be less deep. Third, I did not search exhaustively for conditional or special-case bounds on the least prime value of a polynomial.
